questions.prompt: Why does sin x have no inverse on all real numbers, and on which restricted domain does it have one?
questions.prompt_markup: Why does sin x have no inverse on all real numbers, and on which restricted domain does it have one?

choices.text: sin repeats values, so it is not one-to-one; on 0 ≤ x ≤ π it is increasing and takes each value in [-1, 1] once.
sin is not defined for all real numbers; on 0 ≤ x ≤ π it is defined and takes each value in [-1, 1] once.
sin repeats values, so it is not one-to-one; on -π/2 ≤ x ≤ π/2 it is increasing and takes each value in [-1, 1] once.
sin has outputs greater than 1 for large x; on -π ≤ x ≤ π it takes each value in [-1, 1] exactly once.

questions.correct_answer: sin repeats values, so it is not one-to-one; on -π/2 ≤ x ≤ π/2 it is increasing and takes each value in [-1, 1] once.
questions.grading_note: On [0, π] sin rises then falls; on [-π, π] values repeat. The others use [0, π] or [-π, π], where values repeat, or claim false facts about the domain and outputs of sin.

questions.prompt: What is the standard restricted domain of cos x, and why does it work?
questions.prompt_markup: What is the standard restricted domain of cos x, and why does it work?

choices.text: 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π: cos takes every value from -1 to 1 there, so it is enough.
0 ≤ x ≤ π: cos decreases from 1 to -1 there, taking each value once.
-π/2 ≤ x ≤ π/2: cos increases from -1 to 1 there, taking each value once.
-π ≤ x ≤ 0: cos decreases from 1 to -1 there, taking each value once.

questions.correct_answer: 0 ≤ x ≤ π: cos decreases from 1 to -1 there, taking each value once.
questions.grading_note: On [-π/2, π/2] cos rises and falls; on [-π, 0] it increases. The others use [-π/2, π/2], where cos rises then falls, [0, 2π], where values repeat, or [-π, 0], where cos increases.

questions.prompt: What is the standard restricted domain of tan x, and why does it work?
questions.prompt_markup: What is the standard restricted domain of tan x, and why does it work?

choices.text: -π/2 < x < π/2: tan increases from -∞ to ∞ there, taking each real value once.
0 < x < π: tan is defined and increasing at every point of that interval.
0 ≤ x < π/2: tan increases there and takes each real value exactly once.
-π/2 ≤ x ≤ π/2: tan increases there, including its values at both endpoints.

questions.grading_note: tan is undefined at ±π/2 and takes only nonnegative values on [0, π/2). The others include π/2 (where tan is undefined), include the endpoints ±π/2, or use [0, π/2), which gives only nonnegative values.

questions.prompt: Why must a function be strictly increasing or strictly decreasing on an interval to be invertible there?
questions.prompt_markup: Why must a function be strictly increasing or strictly decreasing on an interval to be invertible there?

choices.text: Then the function is defined at every real number, inside and outside the interval.
Then the function has no zeros on the interval, so it never crosses the x-axis.
Then the outputs are all positive on the interval, so each can be undone.
Then no output repeats on the interval, so each output comes from exactly one input.

questions.correct_answer: Then no output repeats on the interval, so each output comes from exactly one input.
questions.grading_note: Strict monotonicity on an interval implies one-to-one there. The others name properties (domain, zeros, positive outputs) that do not make a function one-to-one.

choices.text: arccos c gives the solution in (0, π); the other is 2π - arccos c, by symmetry over the x-axis.
arccos c gives both solutions at once, because its range is the whole interval [0, 2π).
arccos c gives the solution in (0, π); the other is π - arccos c, by symmetry over the y-axis.
arccos c gives the solution in (-π/2, π/2); the other is arccos c + π, by periodicity.

questions.correct_answer: arccos c gives the solution in (0, π); the other is 2π - arccos c, by symmetry over the x-axis.
questions.grading_note: cos is even: cos(2π - a) = cos(-a) = cos a.
